archetype.name: Super Bowl Contender (offense-first)
archetype.definition: A team whose 9-1 record rests on the league's best net efficiency, driven by the most productive passing game in football and a run defense that takes away the ground game, even if a perfect close-game record overstates the margin.

report.headline: Real contender built on Purdy's efficiency, though close wins flatter the 9-1
report.take:
This is the most efficient team in the league, not just a team with a shiny record. San Francisco ranks first in net EPA (0.227), and the play-by-play has its offense first in EPA per play, first in pass EPA (0.322) and first in success rate. It looks like the 2023 team, which also led the league in net EPA, more than last year's 12-5 side, which got there on luck with a net EPA that ranked only 15th. Brock Purdy has started every game and the offense runs through three people: George Kittle leads the team in targets, Christian McCaffrey leads in carries and is second in targets, and Mike Evans has been the main outside option since he arrived.

The engine is protection and structure. The line ranks first in sack rate and third in pressure rate allowed, and second in both run success and stuff rate. Purdy gets clean pockets, the run game stays on schedule, and the offense rarely faces the long-yardage downs that wreck drives. On defense the identity is narrower. The 49ers are first in rush EPA allowed (-0.208) and first in explosive runs allowed, so offenses have to throw. Against the pass they are ordinary: 12th in pass EPA allowed, with almost no sacks to speak of.

The record is more generous than the play. Every one-score game has gone their way, including six-point wins over Arizona and Washington, a field-goal win in Seattle and a 46-40 shootout in Dallas. That shows up as 1.91 wins over expected, and the point differential of 110 implies about 7.1 wins rather than nine. The Seattle win in particular came from four takeaways and five sacks on a day the offense turned it over three times. Special teams sit dead last at -3.55 EPA a game, which is part of why games this team controls on a per-play basis end up close.

None of that changes the conclusion: the underlying efficiency is real and backed by history, so this is a top contender whose record has some luck in it rather than a team whose quality is in doubt. The question for the stretch run is the season-ending ankle fracture to right tackle Colton McKivitz, a 93% snap starter on the line that makes everything else work.

strengths.title: League's most efficient passing game
strengths.body: Purdy is running the best pass offense in football by EPA, with the league's top success rate underneath it. A clean pocket and a quarterback who throws to the open man on schedule produce it, so it isn't one or two big plays. Efficiency like this held up for this staff in 2023, so it should last, though losing a starting tackle tests the protection side.

strengths.title: Run game that keeps them on schedule
strengths.body: The ground game doesn't produce huge EPA, but it almost never loses yards: second in run success and stuff rate, fourth in yards before contact. That comes from the blocking, and it is why McCaffrey and Kaelon Black can share the carries without the offense stalling. It should hold as long as the interior stays intact, though the right side now has a replacement.

strengths.title: A run defense that takes the ground away
strengths.body: No defense allows less EPA on the ground, and none gives up fewer explosive runs. Opponents end up one-dimensional, throwing into a secondary that holds up well against deep shots. This is the most reliable part of the defense and it lines up well against run-first opponents.

concerns.title: Perfect close-game record won't hold
concerns.body: Every one-score game has gone San Francisco's way, and the point differential implies about seven wins, not nine. Part of that is turnover swings, like four takeaways in Seattle. Part of it is a last-ranked special teams unit that keeps games closer than the play suggests. Expect a split in the next coin-flip games, which costs wins rather than standing.

concerns.title: Losing the starting right tackle
concerns.body: McKivitz fractured and dislocated his ankle against Minnesota and is out until at least February, after playing 93% of snaps. The protection numbers are the base of the offense, and the one game where they broke down, five sacks in Dallas, shows what happens when they do. How well the replacement holds up decides whether Purdy's efficiency survives intact.

concerns.title: No pass rush, soft spots in coverage
concerns.body: The defense ranks last in sack rate, and pass defense sits mid-pack, with short throws and the slot (WR3 targets) the weak spots. Takeaways have covered for it, but quarterbacks who get the ball out quickly can move the chains, as Dallas did in a 46-40 game. With Lenoir hurt and Hobbs on IR, the coverage depth is thin too.

trend.note: After the four-turnover loss in Atlanta and the bye, the offense posted its two best passing-EPA games of the year, against Dallas and against Minnesota's top-ranked defense. Even the 40 points allowed in Dallas came in a win.

nextGame.headline: Seattle's elite defense meets Purdy, but its offense is running on fumes
nextGame.body:
This is strength against strength on one side of the ball. Seattle's defense is fifth in EPA allowed and first in success rate allowed. It takes away the deep ball and explosive passes better than anyone, and its pressure rate ranks fifth. The cracks are underneath and inside the 20: Seattle ranks 25th on short passes and 29th in red-zone touchdown rate, which suits a Purdy offense that lives on Kittle and McCaffrey. The other side favors San Francisco. Seattle runs more than expected, yet its run game ranks near the bottom in EPA, and it would be pushing that into the league's best run defense. The first meeting was a 32-29 49ers win built on four takeaways and five sacks while their own offense sputtered. The Book has the 49ers by 3 at home with a total of 46.5. An early forecast calls for drizzle and modest wind, worth noting but not a game-changer.

Availability leans San Francisco's way despite its own losses. The 49ers will be without McKivitz for the season, Dre Greenlaw (neck) and Khalid Kareem (ankle) missed the Minnesota game, Nate Hobbs is on IR, and Deommodore Lenoir is listed questionable with a foot injury. Seattle's list is heavier: Sam Darnold is listed out with a quadriceps injury, though he was suited up for Monday's practice, and Drew Lock has made six starts. Guard Quenton Nelson and left tackle Charles Cross are out, right tackle Abraham Lucas is questionable, defensive tackle Leonard Williams is out, Jarran Reed is questionable and running back George Holani is on IR.

waysToWin.title: Strangle a run-first, depleted offense
waysToWin.body: Seattle wants to run, and its run game was already among the league's worst before it lost Nelson, Cross and Holani. Against the best rush defense in football, that leaves a backup-heavy line and possibly Lock in obvious passing downs. Early leads make it worse for them.

waysToWin.title: Win underneath and in the red zone
waysToWin.body: Seattle shuts down deep shots, so the path is the short game where it ranks 25th, with Kittle and McCaffrey as the targets. Drives that reach the red zone should turn into touchdowns against a unit that ranks 29th there, which matters because field goals keep Seattle in it.

waysToWin.title: A quiet pass rush finally gets home
waysToWin.body: The 49ers rarely sack anyone, but Seattle allows the highest pressure rate in the league and is now missing its left tackle and a starting guard. This is the best chance all year for the front to create negative plays and the takeaways that decided the first meeting.

waysToLose.title: A replay of the Week 5 mess
waysToLose.body: In Seattle the 49ers turned it over three times, took three sacks and finished with negative pass and rush EPA. Seattle's pressure ranks fifth, and it now meets a line breaking in a new right tackle. If that matchup breaks down, Purdy's efficiency goes with it.

waysToLose.title: Special teams hand over field position
waysToLose.body: San Francisco has the worst special teams EPA in the league, and Seattle's ranks fifth. In a game the Book sees as a field goal, a short field or a missed kick can decide it. A Seattle offense that struggles to move the ball needs exactly those gifts.

waysToLose.title: Seattle's defense wins third down
waysToLose.body: Seattle ranks third in third-down defense and first in deep-pass EPA allowed. If it keeps the 49ers from extending drives and erases the shots, this becomes a low-possession grind decided by a turnover or two, the one kind of game where a weaker offense can steal a win.

nextGame.watch: How San Francisco's fill-in right tackle holds up against Seattle's pressure on early downs. If Purdy stays clean, the 49ers' short game should outlast a banged-up Seattle offense.

restOfSeason.body:
The efficiency is the sustainable part. A top-ranked passing offense with elite protection and run blocking, plus a run defense that forces offenses into the air, describes a team that should be favored in most of what's left. The schedule splits cleanly: three soft games against the Chargers, Eagles and Cardinals, and four real tests in Seattle, the Giants on the road, the Rams at home and Kansas City on the road. With a three-game lead in the NFC West, the division is theirs to lose.

What regresses is the margin in close games. The perfect one-score record and the gap between nine wins and the 7.1 the differential implies point to a split or a loss or two in the next tight finishes, especially with last-ranked special teams. The McKivitz injury is the biggest variable: if protection slips from elite to average, the offense goes from best in the league to merely very good, and the defense, which lacks a pass rush, won't make up the difference.
swingFactors: Close-game and turnover luck evening out
Health of Lenoir and the secondary

confidence.note: Ten games of league-best efficiency with a track record to match. The right tackle injury is the main unknown.
